plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 4: Motion in Two and Three Dimensions
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a compact three-dimensional vector diagram drawn on a set of coordinate axes. The z-axis rises vertically, the y-axis extends to the right, and the x-axis runs toward the lower left, out of the page; all three are thin black lines with small arrowheads and italic labels, meeting at an unlabeled origin. Two purple dots mark positions in space, P_1 sitting above and to the right of the origin and P_2 lower and farther to the right. A thick purple arrow from the origin to P_1 is labeled r(t_1) and a second purple arrow from the origin to P_2 is labeled r(t_2), both symbols carrying overhead vector arrows. A third purple arrow of the same weight runs directly from P_1 to P_2 and is labeled delta r. The three arrows close into a triangle, so the picture shows the displacement as exactly the vector that must be added to the earlier position vector to arrive at the later one. Casting the difference of two position vectors as a single arrow drawn between the two points extends the one-dimensional idea of displacement to motion anywhere in space.

elements: z-axis: thin black line rising vertically from origin with small arrowhead and italic bold label 'z' at top
y-axis: thin black line from origin to the right with arrowhead and italic bold label 'y' at right end
x-axis: thin black line from origin toward the lower-left (out of the page) with arrowhead and italic bold label 'x' at lower-left end
unlabeled origin point where the three axes meet (left-of-center in the frame)
purple filled dot at P_1, above and to the right of the origin, with italic label 'P₁' set just above-right of the dot
purple filled dot at P_2, farther right and below the y-axis, with italic label 'P₂' set just below-right of the dot
thick purple arrow from origin to P_1, labeled 'r⃗(t₁)' (vector-arrow overbar) below the shaft
thick purple arrow from origin to P_2, labeled 'r⃗(t₂)' (vector-arrow overbar) above the shaft
thick purple arrow from P_1 to P_2, labeled 'Δr⃗' to the right of the shaft
the closed triangle formed by the three purple arrows (origin, P₁, P₂)

interactions.teaches: Moving either P₁ or P₂ redraws both position vectors and the displacement arrow, showing that Δr⃗ is always the arrow that closes the triangle: r⃗(t₁) + Δr⃗ = r⃗(t₂), no matter where the points sit in space.
Rotating the axes reveals that P₁ and P₂ lie at genuinely different depths along x, so the flat-looking triangle is a real 3D configuration.

demo_steps.title: Empty coordinate frame
demo_steps.narration: Only the x, y, z axes and the origin are shown. Positions in space will be specified as vectors drawn from this origin.

demo_steps.title: Initial position r⃗(t₁)
demo_steps.narration: At time t₁ the particle is at P₁; the purple arrow from the origin to P₁ is its position vector r⃗(t₁).

demo_steps.title: Final position r⃗(t₂)
demo_steps.narration: Later, at t₂, the particle is at P₂, with position vector r⃗(t₂) drawn from the same origin.

demo_steps.title: Displacement closes the triangle
demo_steps.narration: The arrow drawn directly from P₁ to P₂ is the displacement Δr⃗ = r⃗(t₂) − r⃗(t₁) — exactly the vector that must be added to the earlier position vector to reach the later one. Drag either point to see the relation hold.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World axes: +X screen-right carries the physics y-axis, +Y screen-up carries the physics z-axis, +Z toward the viewer (drawn receding to lower-left in the standard isometric pose) carries the physics x-axis. Axis lines are thin black (#000000, ~0.015 unit radius or 2px lines) with small cone arrowheads: z-axis from origin up to +3.0, y-axis from origin right to +3.4, x-axis from origin toward viewer to +3.0. Origin sits left-of-center, roughly 30% across the frame. Italic bold labels 'z' above the z arrowhead, 'y' just right of the y arrowhead, 'x' just below the x arrowhead. Default points (physics x, y, z): P₁ = (0.8, 2.2, 1.7) — above and right of origin, clearly above the y-axis line; P₂ = (1.6, 3.1, −0.7) — farther right and below the y-axis line, nearer the viewer. Dots are purple spheres of radius ~0.07. All three vector arrows are thick purple (#8E2D8E, shaft radius ~0.05, cone head length ~0.28, head radius ~0.11). Labels r⃗(t₁) placed just below the midpoint of the origin→P₁ shaft, r⃗(t₂) just above the midpoint of the origin→P₂ shaft, Δr⃗ just right of the midpoint of the P₁→P₂ shaft; all label text purple, italic serif, with an overbar arrow glyph. Δr⃗ must always be computed as P₂ − P₁ so the head lands exactly on P₂. Drag constraint: each point moves in the plane facing the camera (or on a small 3D gizmo), clamped to |coordinate| ≤ 3.4 so it stays inside the axis box.
interactionPlan.notes: Use an orthographic camera in a standard isometric pose for the axonometric look. Build each vector as a group of CylinderGeometry shaft + ConeGeometry head, oriented with quaternion setFromUnitVectors from +Y to the normalized vector, rescaled on every update rather than rebuilt. Labels as CSS2DRenderer/HTML sprites with MathJax or unicode overbar so they stay screen-aligned and crisp during orbit. Axes as thin Line/TubeGeometry in black with small cones; render the negative side of each axis short or not at all, matching the source. Draggable points use a raycaster against an invisible plane through the point normal to the camera; show a faint dashed projection to the xy-plane only while dragging to reinforce depth. The state interaction fades vectors in/out by animating opacity and shaft length (0→1) over ~400 ms.

authoredContext:
With our definition of the position of a particle in three-dimensional space, we can formulate the three-dimensional displacement. The figure shows a particle at time t1 located at P1 with position vector r→(t1). At a later time t2, the particle is located at P2 with position vector r→(t2). The displacement vector Δr→ is found by subtracting r→(t1) from r→(t2):

Vector addition is discussed in Vectors. Note that this is the same operation we did in one dimension, but now the vectors are in three-dimensional space.

The displacement Δr→=r→(t2)−r→(t1) is the vector from P1 to P2.

An x y z coordinate system is shown, with positive x out of the page, positive y to the right, and positive z up. Two points, P 1 and P 2 are shown. The vector r of t 1 from the origin to P 1 and the vector r of t 2 from the origin to P 2 are shown as purple arrows. The vector delta r is shown as a purple arrow whose tail is at P 1 and head at P 2.

The following examples illustrate the concept of displacement in multiple dimensions.

Build the displacement
Guided demo
Points (physics x, y, z)
Drag either purple dot to move it in the plane facing you — both position vectors and Δr⃗ redraw so the triangle always closes.
Drag the background to orbit and see that P₁ and P₂ sit at different depths along x.
⚠ Figure failed to load

discrepancies: Camera/axis orientation is wrong: in the source the y-axis runs horizontally to the right, x-axis toward the lower-left and the whole triangle sits in the upper-right quadrant; in the render the x-axis points left and y-axis to the lower-right, so the frame appears mirrored/rotated relative to the source.

Because of the chosen view direction the three purple arrows project almost onto a single near-vertical line — the characteristic closed triangle (r⃗(t₁), r⃗(t₂), Δr⃗) of the source figure is essentially invisible, destroying the figure's key visual message.
P₁ and P₂ are placed far too close together on screen and P₂ falls well below the y-axis, whereas the source has P₁ above the y-axis and P₂ just below it with a wide, clearly separated triangle.
The r⃗(t₁) and r⃗(t₂) labels are crammed on top of each other near the origin and are visually truncated/overlapped by the arrow shafts; in the source they sit clearly along the middle of each arrow.
UI button text shows the vector-arrow combining character as a tofu box ("r□(t₁)", "Δr□"), a rendering/typography defect in the control panel.
Arrow shafts are rendered as very thick cylinders relative to the axis lines, heavier than the thin, tapered strokes of the source diagram.
evaluation.notes: The underlying physics (position vectors and the closing displacement triangle) and the staged/draggable interactions are well conceived, but the default camera orientation projects the three arrows nearly onto a single line and flips the x/y screen directions, so the resulting image barely resembles the source triangle figure.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction design are sound (concept 4, interactivity 4); the problems are implementation-level — default camera orientation, point spacing/scale, label placement, arrow thickness, and a font glyph issue in the UI.

discrepancies: Arrow shafts are far thicker relative to their length than in the source, where all three purple vectors are drawn as slender lines with small heads — the generated triangle reads as heavy bars rather than vectors.
The vector-arrow glyph (combining arrow U+20D7) renders as tofu boxes ('r□(t₁)', 'Δr□') in the control-panel buttons and numeric readout, so the key notation r⃗ / Δr⃗ is broken in the UI text.
The Δr⃗ label sits on the midpoint of the displacement arrow and collides with the y-axis line; in the source it is offset clearly to the right of the arrow, away from the axis.

Overall scene is smaller/lower in frame than the source composition — the triangle hangs well below the y-axis tip and the axes occupy a smaller share of the canvas than the printed figure, and the x-axis arrowhead reads as a small blob rather than a clear arrow.
evaluation.notes: Faithful 3D reconstruction of the position/displacement triangle with a correct axonometric viewpoint and genuinely useful staged build, drag-the-endpoint, and readout interactions; weakened by over-thick arrow shafts, a Δr⃗ label overlapping the y-axis, and broken vector-arrow glyphs (tofu boxes) in the panel text.
action_items: Reduce arrow shaft radius (≈0.02–0.03) and head size so the vectors look like thin drawn arrows as in the source.
Replace the U+20D7 combining arrow in HTML panel text/buttons with a rendered overline (e.g. r) or SVG glyph so 'r⃗(t₁)', 'r⃗(t₂)', 'Δr⃗' display correctly.
Offset the Δr⃗ label perpendicular to the displacement arrow (to the right, as in the source) so it no longer sits on the y-axis line.
Increase scene scale slightly (larger heightFraction / axis lengths) and enlarge the x-axis arrowhead so the triad matches the printed figure's prominence.

plan.contextChunk: This figure is a compact three-dimensional vector diagram drawn on a set of coordinate axes. The z-axis rises vertically, the y-axis extends to the right, and the x-axis runs toward the lower left, out of the page; all three are thin black lines with small arrowheads and italic labels, meeting at an unlabeled origin. Two purple dots mark positions in space, P_1 sitting above and to the right of the origin and P_2 lower and farther to the right. A thick purple arrow from the origin to P_1 is labeled r(t_1) and a second purple arrow from the origin to P_2 is labeled r(t_2), both symbols carrying overhead vector arrows. A third purple arrow of the same weight runs directly from P_1 to P_2 and is labeled delta r. The three arrows close into a triangle, so the picture shows the displacement as exactly the vector that must be added to the earlier position vector to arrive at the later one. Casting the difference of two position vectors as a single arrow drawn between the two points extends the one-dimensional idea of displacement to motion anywhere in space.

elements: z-axis: thin black line rising vertically from origin with small arrowhead and italic bold label 'z' at top
y-axis: thin black line from origin to the right with arrowhead and italic bold label 'y' at right end
x-axis: thin black line from origin toward the lower-left (out of the page) with arrowhead and italic bold label 'x' at lower-left end
unlabeled origin point where the three axes meet (left-of-center in the frame)
purple filled dot at P_1, above and to the right of the origin, with italic label 'P₁' set just above-right of the dot
purple filled dot at P_2, farther right and below the y-axis, with italic label 'P₂' set just below-right of the dot
thick purple arrow from origin to P_1, labeled 'r⃗(t₁)' (vector-arrow overbar) below the shaft
thick purple arrow from origin to P_2, labeled 'r⃗(t₂)' (vector-arrow overbar) above the shaft
thick purple arrow from P_1 to P_2, labeled 'Δr⃗' to the right of the shaft
the closed triangle formed by the three purple arrows (origin, P₁, P₂)

interactions.teaches: Moving either P₁ or P₂ redraws both position vectors and the displacement arrow, showing that Δr⃗ is always the arrow that closes the triangle: r⃗(t₁) + Δr⃗ = r⃗(t₂), no matter where the points sit in space.
Rotating the axes reveals that P₁ and P₂ lie at genuinely different depths along x, so the flat-looking triangle is a real 3D configuration.

demo_steps.title: Empty coordinate frame
demo_steps.narration: Only the x, y, z axes and the origin are shown. Positions in space will be specified as vectors drawn from this origin.

demo_steps.title: Initial position r⃗(t₁)
demo_steps.narration: At time t₁ the particle is at P₁; the purple arrow from the origin to P₁ is its position vector r⃗(t₁).

demo_steps.title: Final position r⃗(t₂)
demo_steps.narration: Later, at t₂, the particle is at P₂, with position vector r⃗(t₂) drawn from the same origin.

demo_steps.title: Displacement closes the triangle
demo_steps.narration: The arrow drawn directly from P₁ to P₂ is the displacement Δr⃗ = r⃗(t₂) − r⃗(t₁) — exactly the vector that must be added to the earlier position vector to reach the later one. Drag either point to see the relation hold.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World axes: +X screen-right carries the physics y-axis, +Y screen-up carries the physics z-axis, +Z toward the viewer (drawn receding to lower-left in the standard isometric pose) carries the physics x-axis. Axis lines are thin black (#000000, ~0.015 unit radius or 2px lines) with small cone arrowheads: z-axis from origin up to +3.0, y-axis from origin right to +3.4, x-axis from origin toward viewer to +3.0. Origin sits left-of-center, roughly 30% across the frame. Italic bold labels 'z' above the z arrowhead, 'y' just right of the y arrowhead, 'x' just below the x arrowhead. Default points (physics x, y, z): P₁ = (0.8, 2.2, 1.7) — above and right of origin, clearly above the y-axis line; P₂ = (1.6, 3.1, −0.7) — farther right and below the y-axis line, nearer the viewer. Dots are purple spheres of radius ~0.07. All three vector arrows are thick purple (#8E2D8E, shaft radius ~0.05, cone head length ~0.28, head radius ~0.11). Labels r⃗(t₁) placed just below the midpoint of the origin→P₁ shaft, r⃗(t₂) just above the midpoint of the origin→P₂ shaft, Δr⃗ just right of the midpoint of the P₁→P₂ shaft; all label text purple, italic serif, with an overbar arrow glyph. Δr⃗ must always be computed as P₂ − P₁ so the head lands exactly on P₂. Drag constraint: each point moves in the plane facing the camera (or on a small 3D gizmo), clamped to |coordinate| ≤ 3.4 so it stays inside the axis box.
interactionPlan.notes: Use an orthographic camera in a standard isometric pose for the axonometric look. Build each vector as a group of CylinderGeometry shaft + ConeGeometry head, oriented with quaternion setFromUnitVectors from +Y to the normalized vector, rescaled on every update rather than rebuilt. Labels as CSS2DRenderer/HTML sprites with MathJax or unicode overbar so they stay screen-aligned and crisp during orbit. Axes as thin Line/TubeGeometry in black with small cones; render the negative side of each axis short or not at all, matching the source. Draggable points use a raycaster against an invisible plane through the point normal to the camera; show a faint dashed projection to the xy-plane only while dragging to reinforce depth. The state interaction fades vectors in/out by animating opacity and shaft length (0→1) over ~400 ms.

discrepancies: The Δr label sits essentially on top of the y-axis line (left of its arrow) rather than clearly outside the triangle to the right of the P₁→P₂ arrow as in the source, weakening its association with the displacement vector.
Vector notation uses an overline (r̄) instead of the source's arrow-over-r (r⃗); physically an overline conventionally means an average, so the notation is not faithful to the printed figure.

The y-axis is rendered sloping slightly downward to the right rather than horizontal as printed, and the x-axis arrowhead renders as a near-head-on black blob instead of a clean arrow, slightly muddying the axonometric triad.

Minor proportion difference: the source's r(t₁) reaches a P₁ noticeably higher relative to the y-axis and the triangle is more compact; the generated triangle is stretched further down-right toward P₂.
evaluation.notes: A faithful, genuinely 3D reconstruction of the position/displacement vector triangle with excellent staged build, draggable endpoints and live component readout; main weaknesses are the overline-instead-of-arrow vector notation, a Δr label that lands on the y-axis line, and a slightly tilted y-axis with a blobby x-axis arrowhead.
